Notes: Presence (cemetery): Science News (B. Bower, 17 Nov 2017) reports IAA anthropologist Y. Nagar's analysis of 33 skeletons newly excavated in the Qumran cemetery by H. Hizmi and Y. Aharonovich (2016) plus reexamination of 53 earlier skeletons; 30 of the new individuals definitely or probably male, aged c. 20 to 50+, a few children; preliminary radiocarbon date of one bone c. 2,200 years old (Year of Data c. -183 derived from that, approximate). Burials of the site's residents; no community size given. Year Established -700 = earliest Judahite presence (Iron Age II remains of the 8th-7th c. BCE, incl. an LMLK seal impression, midpoint -700; see Encyclopaedia Judaica and COJS rows).

Event/founding: Encyclopaedia Judaica (encyclopedia.com) - after Iron Age II walls and pottery (8th-7th c. BCE; basis of Year Established -700), the Second Temple settlement's phase Ia 'may have been constructed by John Hyrcanus I (134-104 BCE) or more likely by one of his predecessors' (year = midpoint of Hyrcanus' reign, c.). The site is described as the headquarters of 'a fairly large and well-organized community', identified by de Vaux with the Essenes (a Jewish sect); no population figure; cemetery of c. 1,200 graves.

Event/presence: COJS excavation overview - earliest finds from the Israelite monarchy (8th-7th c. BCE); Period Ia generally placed around the Maccabean period; main occupation Period Ib 'began somewhere around the reign of Alexander Janneus (103-76 BCE)', possibly under John Hyrcanus (c. -100). Water system filled the 'mikvaot (ritual baths)'; the water system and large dining hall indicate a large population but few rooms; Qumran-type pottery in Cave 1 (scroll cave); graves of women and children alongside many male graves. Jewish sectarian community, no count.

Presence (coins): Wikipedia 'Qumran coins' - de Vaux's excavations (1951-56) found about 1,250 coins and Magen & Peleg 259 more; 'most of the coins... belonged to the time of Alexander Jannaeus' (103-76 BCE; Hasmonean period midpoint -90 used). Hasmonean Jewish coinage in the settlement attests occupation; no count.

Scholarly estimate (Y. Hirschfeld, Qumran in Context, 2004, as summarized by Wikipedia): applying a low density coefficient of about 15 persons per dunam derived from other ancient settlements, only about 20 people occupied Qumran in the Hasmonean period (Hasmonean midpoint -90). Hirschfeld saw Qumran as a fortified manor/farm, but the residents are Judeans. Wikipedia used as last resort; original book not accessed.

Event/presence: D. Stacey (Bible and Interpretation, June 2004) - a 7th c. BCE Judahite fort guarded a track to the Buqei'a; the Hasmoneans renovated the Iron Age cistern in the late reign of John Hyrcanus or early Alexander Janneus; the garrison 'may have been withdrawn as early as c. 80 B.C.E.', after which 'a profusion of miqva'ot gradually surrounded and encroached into the earlier structure'; some residents were potters, others perhaps acolytes of the Essene sect. Over a thousand burials, 'too many for them all to have lived and died there'. No count.

Presence (main period): G. Doudna, 'Deconstructing the Continuity of Qumran Ib and II' (2016, excerpts) argues the 'true main period of activity at Qumran was mid- and late-first century BCE' (Period Ib), when the people of the site deposited the (Hebrew and Aramaic) scrolls in the nearby caves; argues against continuity of the same community into Period II. No count; 1st c. BCE midpoint -50.

Event: Encyclopaedia Judaica - phase Ib 'was terminated by a severe earthquake (almost certainly the famous one of 31 b.c.e.) followed by an extensive fire' (Josephus, War 1.370-80). Damage to the settlement; per de Vaux followed by abandonment (see -15 row).

Scholarly estimate (E.-M. Laperrousaz, as summarized by Wikipedia): up to 1,428 inhabitants; generally regarded as excessively high (Wikipedia: proposals other than Laperrousaz range c. 20-200). Year = midpoint of main sectarian occupation c. 100 BCE-68 CE (c.). Original not accessed.

Scholarly estimate (R. de Vaux, as summarized by Wikipedia): from the size of the cemetery and average lifespan, the inhabitants 'would not have numbered many more than 200 members'; he noted the graves far exceeded what the buildings could house and wondered whether caves were used for lodging. Year = midpoint of main occupation c. 100 BCE-68 CE (c.). Jewish sectarian settlement.

Scholarly estimate (J.T. Milik, as summarized by Wikipedia): average population of 150-200 (midpoint 175), by comparison with the c. 150 monks of Mar Saba and Josephus' 3,000 Essenes, assuming at least 5% lived a strict communal life. Year = midpoint of main occupation (c.).

Scholarly estimate (M. Broshi, 'The Archaeology of Qumran - A Reconsideration', 113-14, cited by R. Hachlili, 'The Qumran Cemetery: A Reconsideration'): community of about 150-200 (midpoint 175); Wikipedia summarizes Broshi's basis as 120-150 seats in the assembly hall (L77) plus a few dozen candidates (over 170); J. Magness accepted it given >1,000 dishes in pantry L86. Hachlili: cemetery of 1,100-1,200 graves used c. 190 years (Periods Ib-II, 2nd half of 2nd c. BCE to 68 CE). Year = midpoint of main occupation (c.).

Scholarly estimate (J. Patrich, 'Khirbet Qumran in Light of New Archaeological Explorations in the Qumran Caves', 1994, cited by R. Hachlili): 50-70 inhabitants (midpoint 60), based on cave surveys showing caves were not dwellings, so residents lived within the buildings. Year = midpoint of main occupation (c.).

Scholarly estimate (M. Broshi and H. Eshel, cave and tent survey 1995-96, as summarized by Wikipedia): they first judged the building could hold only 12-20 people, then, counting residential caves and tents (pottery and nails along paths), kept the total at 150-200 (midpoint 175). Patrich rejected the tent/nail evidence. Year = midpoint of main occupation (c.).

Scholarly estimate (J.-B. Humbert, as reported by R. Gmirkin, orion list, 7 Dec 2000, citing Patrich): 10-15 residents at Qumran (midpoint 12.5, rounded). Gmirkin himself suggests 10-40 incl. 3-6 in marl caves, and notes estimates of 150-200 would require most to live outside the site. Year = midpoint of main occupation (c.).

Scholarly estimates (range, no single figure): A. Rabinovich, Jerusalem Post, 25 July 1997 (orion list): 'Estimates of Qumran's population ranged from 50 or less to 150 or more'; Hirschfeld and Patrich, holding that all residents lived inside the walled structure, 'reckoned that they numbered no more than 50'; Broshi calculated only c. 80 m2 of living space in the compound, room for 'no more than 12 people at best', the rest living in caves/tents (12 is a subset, not the total). Population left blank: only upper bounds/subsets.

Scholarly assessment (J. Patrich, research projects page): the 'permanent population residing there could not count more than few dozens'; caves were not permanent dwellings; the refectory 'could have served ca. 150 inhabitants or more' because sect members from Jerusalem came for feasts; Qumran 'an integral part of the Essene community of Jerusalem'. Population blank (no exact figure; upper bound of a few dozen). Year = midpoint of main occupation (c.).

Documented absence (de Vaux's chronology, as quoted from Magness 2002 on deadseaquake.info): 'Qumran lay in ruins and was unoccupied for about 30 years after the earthquake of 31 B.C.E.'; Period II resumed c. 4-1 BCE. Year = c. midpoint of the gap. Disputed: Magness reduced the gap to 'one winter season to several years' and Mizzi & Magness 2016 argue for continuous occupation (see rows -9 and -6).

Event: G. Doudna (2016) summarizing J. Magness - a hoard of Tyrian silver tetradrachms (latest coin 9/8 BCE) was buried in Locus 120; Magness dates the end of Period Ib to '9/8 BCE or some time thereafter', a crisis (destruction by fire, possibly in the upheavals near Herod's death), followed by abandonment of uncertain length and resettlement (Period II). Year c. -9. No count.

Scholarly reassessment: D. Mizzi and J. Magness, 'Was Qumran Abandoned at the End of the First Century BCE?' (JBL 135/2, 2016; abstract) reject the destruction/abandonment c. 9/8 BCE and reoccupation c. 4/1 BCE and propose 'collapsing Periods I and II into one long phase of occupation', i.e. continuous Jewish occupation across the turn of the era. Year c. -6 (period in question). No count.

Event: COJS - Period II resettlement; 'Numismatic evidence places this occupation at the time of Herod Archelaus... (4 BCE to 6 CE)' (year c. 1, midpoint). Period II ended when the Romans destroyed Qumran during the Great Revolt. No count.

Scholarly estimate (Y. Magen and Y. Peleg, IAA excavations 1993-2004, reported by Y. Ben-Ami, Bible and Interpretation, Oct 2004): 'about 25 people at any given time'; they see Qumran as a Hasmonean fortress, later (after 63 BCE) a pottery factory; Hirschfeld dates the first phase to c. 100 BCE and suggests 'a few dozen'; supporters of the monastery theory estimate over 100. Ben-Ami: 'no question as to the Jewishness of the ancient inhabitants'. Year = early Roman period midpoint (4).

Presence (material culture): Y. Ben-Ami (Bible and Interpretation, 2004) - stone vessels 'used by Jews of the period so they could abide by the Jewish purity laws' and 'pottery sherds... inscribed with Jewish names' found at the site; stepped cisterns interpreted by many as mikva'ot (disputed by Magen). Indicates a Jewish resident group of modest size. Year = early Roman midpoint (c.).

Presence: FARMS Insights 16/1 (1996) - H. Eshel and M. Broshi, excavating caves outside the ruins, 'identified a residential quarter' 'inhabited by the Dead Sea sect 2,000 years ago' (dated only c.; early Roman midpoint used). Suggests residents living outside the main building; no count.

Scholarly estimate (J. Patrich at the 1997 Jerusalem congress, reported by F. Cryer, orion list, 2 Feb 1998): dwellings demonstrably inhabited in the 1st c. CE (excluding storage and production facilities) 'only leave room for a settlement consisting of ca. 12-15 people' (midpoint 13.5, rounded). Year = 1st c. CE midpoint.

Presence (ostracon): S. Goranson (orion list, 14 Aug 1997) on the ostracon found at Qumran in 1996 and published by F.M. Cross and E. Eshel (IEJ 47 [1997] 17-28) as 'a first century CE Essene deed of gift', dated 'year 2' - which the editors relate to year 2 of the First Revolt (67/68 CE), a reading Goranson questions; others (Yardeni) reject the 'yahad' reading. Year c. 67. Records a property gift by a Jewish resident; no count.

Presence (revolt coins): Wikipedia 'Qumran coins' - 'bronze coins... some dating to the second and third years of the Jewish War, indicate that the site was still actively in use in 68 CE and only destroyed after 70, perhaps as late as 73'; two small hoards with terminal years 68-69 CE. Jewish rebel-era coinage in the settlement; no count.

Event: Encyclopaedia Judaica - phase II 'came to an end during the First Revolt, in the year 68 c.e.'; per de Vaux the building was 'attacked and stormed by the Romans in the summer of 68 c.e.' (Vespasian's campaign near Jericho). Destruction of the Jewish settlement.

Documented end of the community: M. Broshi (quoted on deadseaquake.info): 'This is the end of stratum II - that is, summer 68 CE - the date the Qumran community ceased to exist.' Afterwards (Period III, to c. 73 CE) the site was used by Roman forces (COJS). Some coin evidence suggests use after 70 (see 68 row), so the date of the end is debated.
